name: London English (Cockney and Multicultural London English)
summary: This file keeps two different London varieties apart. COCKNEY is the traditional (older) East End working-class accent: TH-fronting, glottal stop for t, L-vocalisation, h-dropping, non-rhoticity, 'me' for 'my', 'ain't', double negatives, and rhyming slang. MULTICULTURAL LONDON ENGLISH (MLE) is the newer sociolect of many young Londoners of diverse backgrounds: both th-stopping and th-fronting occur, innit is its only tag, 'was' is levelled, 'man' works as a pronoun, 'this is' can introduce quotations, FACE/PRICE/MOUTH vowels are different, and intonation has a distinctive rise-fall. Round 2 corrected two round-1 points: (1) MLE is not 'th-stopping only'; the MLE article lists both stopping and fronting, so do not give a hard rule; (2) 'kosher' and 'Mockney' were removed (kosher is not London-specific; Mockney describes a fake accent, not a word to put in a character's mouth). Evidence still leans on Wikipedia summaries of Cheshire, Kerswill, Fox and Torgersen and others, plus a 2026 York/QMUL study on MLE intonation and the Cheshire et al. 2011 abstract. Primary articles beyond abstracts were not read in full.

grammar.standard: is not / are not / am not / has not
grammar.condition: COCKNEY, informal. Used for be and have negatives (source 1).
COCKNEY. Wikipedia gives the example 'At's me book you got 'ere' (source 1). Older / traditional speakers.
grammar.example_standard: That's my book you've got there.
grammar.example_dialect: That's me book you've got there.

grammar.condition: COCKNEY. Wikipedia gives 'I didn't see nuffink' as an example, showing both th-fronting and double negative (source 1). Also found in other working-class speech.

MLE: past 'be' is levelled (was in positives; weren't in negatives is reported) and the choice is linked to ethnicity and gender: non-standard 'was' is highest among Black Caribbean-heritage speakers and lowest among Bangladeshi-heritage speakers (Cheshire and Fox 2008 via source 2). Do not give it to every character.
MLE: 'innit' is the (only) tag; it can also mark a topic or stress new information, not just ask for confirmation (Cheshire, Nortier and Adger 2015 via source 2).
MLE: 'man' can be used as a first-person singular pronoun and sometimes for second or third person (Cheshire 2013 via source 2). Example sentence is constructed.

grammar.dialect: and this is (+ subject), e.g. 'this is me, ...'
grammar.condition: MLE, drama-telling: 'this is' introduces direct speech in dramatic scenes (Cheshire, Hall and Adger 2017 via source 2). BE LIKE is also a main youth quotative (source 5). Optional, once at most. Example constructed.
grammar.example_dialect: And this is me, 'What's your problem?'

grammar.condition: MLE: 'still' at the end of a sentence, alone or with 'though', to seek agreement or soften (Cheshire, Adams and Hall 2024 via source 2). Low-to-medium confidence; example constructed.

Traditional southern English, most common in white female speakers in the data (Kerswill 2007 via source 2).

pronunciation.rule: COCKNEY TH-fronting: th becomes f, and voiced th becomes v (not at the start of a word).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Lower lip to upper teeth: 'thin' -> 'fin', 'bath' -> 'baf', 'brother' -> 'bruvver'. Keep 'this' / 'the' with an ordinary start.

pronunciation.rule: MLE th: BOTH th-stopping (thing -> ting, this -> dis) and th-fronting (three -> free, brother -> bruver) are listed for MLE (source 2). Round 1 said MLE = stopping only; that was too strong.
pronunciation.actor_tip: For an MLE character choose ONE pattern and use it lightly. Stopping: tongue tip on the back of the upper teeth. Do not use it for every character.

pronunciation.rule: COCKNEY glottal stop: t in the middle or end of words is replaced by a catch in the throat. In MLE a medial/final t is only variably glottal.
pronunciation.actor_tip: 'Hyde Park' -> 'Hy' Par''. The air stops for a moment as in 'uh-oh'. Do not apply it to word-initial t or every t.

pronunciation.rule: COCKNEY L-vocalisation: dark l at the end of a word or before a consonant turns into a w-like vowel. The MLE article does not list this feature.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Round the lips as for 'w'; do not touch the tongue tip. Use for Cockney only.

pronunciation.rule: COCKNEY diphthongs: MOUTH a long flat vowel; FACE a front 'a' gliding to y; PRICE starts at 'ah' and glides up; GOAT starts at 'uh' and glides to 'oo'.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Practise each word separately first: 'mouth' (long flat 'a'), 'face' ('fay-ece' with a low start), 'price', 'goat' ('guh-oot').

pronunciation.rule: COCKNEY h-dropping: initial /h/ is dropped, but can be restored for emphasis. MLE: h-dropping has declined and many speakers pronounce h.
pronunciation.actor_tip: 'house' -> 'ouse'; restore the h on an emphasised word.

pronunciation.rule: COCKNEY yod-coalescence: tune -> choon, duke -> jook.
Non-rhoticity: /r/ not pronounced after a vowel at the end of a word or before a consonant (Cockney and MLE, like most of England).
COCKNEY strong aspiration of p, t, k (word-initial).
pronunciation.actor_tip: Add a puff of air to initial p, t, k when stressed.

pronunciation.rule: MLE FACE: onset raised to [eɪ]-like; monophthong [eː] is strongest in speakers of Black and minority ethnic background (BAME). MLE PRICE: lowered and fronted, sometimes a monophthong [aː] (also strongest in BAME speakers).
pronunciation.actor_tip: 'day' and 'time' with less glide than RP; only for MLE.

pronunciation.rule: MLE MOUTH: [aː] is the default in inner London; some BAME speakers (especially women) use [ɑʊ].
pronunciation.actor_tip: 'now' / 'down' as a long 'aa' without the 'oo' glide.

pronunciation.rule: MLE GOOSE and FOOT fronting: /uː/ is strongly fronted (sometimes [ʏː]); /ʊ/ is fronted too, more in outer London (Havering) than inner (Hackney). GOOSE fronting is one of the two most widespread youth features (Cheshire et al. 2011 abstract, source 5).
MLE GOAT: fronting of the end of /oʊ/ is absent for most inner-city speakers and present in some outer-city girls (source 2). Do not give inner-London MLE characters a fronted GOAT.
MLE K-backing: k before back vowels is produced further back (cousin, come) [q]-like.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Subtle; skip unless you have a recording.

intonation.rule: MLE: the most common nuclear contour is a RISE-FALL; it is near-ubiquitous on yes/no questions and on emphatically lengthened words. It is the same contour as in other English varieties but used far more often (Hellmuth and Passoni 2026, sources 6, 7).
intonation.actor_tip: For MLE questions, rise then fall on the key word, instead of a plain rise.

intonation.rule: MLE emphatic consonant lengthening: a word-initial consonant (p, t, k type) is stretched for dramatic effect (study example: 'meedy' with long m); more by male teens (sources 6, 7).
intonation.actor_tip: Lengthen the first consonant of the emphasised word, once per speech.

intonation.rule: MLE declarative questions ('She's your friend?') without inversion, matching Caribbean-creole patterns (source 6).
intonation.actor_tip: Make a statement and let the question come from rising pitch, not word order.

common_mistakes: Using Cockney and MLE features together on one character. Choose one: Cockney (older East End) or MLE (young, diverse).
Giving MLE speakers Cockney's L-vocalisation and h-dropping. The MLE article does not list L-vocalisation, and h-dropping has declined.
Treating th-fronting as Cockney-only and th-stopping as the only MLE pattern. Both are reported for MLE (source 2).
Over-using 'innit', 'bare', 'peak', 'wagwan' in one speech, or giving MLE slang to older characters.
Using 'guv'nor', 'blimey', 'cor' or 'cushty' as Cockney signals in modern scenes. Caricature, unverified.
Using 'kosher' as London slang. It is not London-specific and was removed.
Respelling with eye-dialect (nuffink, 'ouse, innit as 'init'). Keep standard spelling; carry the sounds in notes.
Putting 'was' levelling on every MLE character; it varies by ethnicity and gender.
generational_notes: Source 1: traditional Cockney features are declining in multicultural areas and being replaced among the young by MLE; a 2010 Kerswill report predicted Cockney would disappear in about 30 years (a prediction, not a fact).

Source 2: older Londoners are closer to the Cockney system, younger speakers show MLE features (Cheshire et al. 2011, 2013). MLE is mostly working-class youth speech and is imitated by some middle-class speakers.

Source 5 (Cheshire et al. 2011 abstract): the features that clearly distinguish the youngest speakers are BE LIKE and GOOSE-fronting; age differences in other features come from community-internal factors.
Intonation: no age difference was found between 2005 and 2024 recordings of Caribbean-heritage MLE speakers (source 6): a stable feature.
Rhyming slang: only 'butcher's' is stated as widely used; others are older or nostalgic.
conversion_guidelines: Natural spoken film-dialogue English first. Decide the character: Cockney (older East End, working class) or MLE (young, multicultural). Never mix.
Cockney: ain't, 'me' for 'my', one double negative, th-fronting + glottal t + h-dropping in notes; maybe one rhyming-slang word (butcher's) with the rhyme dropped.
MLE: innit as a tag, one of 'bare / peak / allow it / wagwan', optional 'man' pronoun or 'this is' quotative once; 'was' levelling only if the character fits.
Choose ONE th pattern for MLE (stopping or fronting) and use it lightly.
MLE intonation: use the rise-fall on emphatic questions and a lengthened first consonant on one word, rather than writing slang into every line.
No eye-dialect respelling. No stock phrases (guv'nor, blimey, cor). No gun/knife slang.
Limit to 2-3 sound rules per monologue. In actor notes, state which variety was applied.

open_questions: Primary articles (Cheshire et al. 2011 full text; Cheshire and Fox 2008; Cheshire 2013, 2017; Kerswill 2007) were not read in full, only through the Wikipedia article and an abstract. Check them before treating any MLE grammar item as certain.
Whether th-stopping or th-fronting is more typical of MLE is not settled in the opened sources. The MLE article lists both.
Cockney intonation: no verified description found. Needs Wells (1982) or the British Library 'Sounds Familiar' pages (the BL page URL tried returned 404).
The 'this is' quotative frequency (about 5% of youth quotatives per a search-result summary of Cheshire and Fox) was not opened; example sentence is constructed.
'Man' pronoun, 'still' and 'Why ... for?' examples are constructed from the rule descriptions, not quotes.
Rhyming slang: only butcher's is stated as widely current; the Wikipedia article is flagged as disputed/needs citations. Check Ayto (Oxford Dictionary of Rhyming Slang) before adding more.
Which words are age-marked (cushty, wonga) was not verified; labels are coaching judgement.
MLE vocabulary also includes gun/knife slang in the source; deliberately omitted.
Th-stopping/glottal-t in 'Jamaican-heritage speakers' per source 2 is a narrow claim; not used as a general rule.

sub_regions.name: Cockney vs MLE
sub_regions.note: Cockney는 런던 동부 노동계층의 전통 말투로 th-fronting, glottal stop, l-vocalisation, h-dropping이 특징. MLE는 다문화 지역 젊은층의 새로운 사회방언이며 영어·자메이카 영어·여러 이민 언어의 접촉에서 형성됨. 한 인물에 섞지 마세요.

sub_regions.note: Cockney와 표준 영국 발음의 중간 억양으로 1980~90년대 런던 주변 남동부로 퍼졌다고 설명됩니다(출처 1).

confidence_detail: medium for Cockney features and MLE grammar (Wikipedia summaries of named academic studies); medium-high for MLE intonation (two 2026 academic pages); low for rhyming slang currency and the 'this is' quotative, 'still' and 'Why ... for?' items.
